spanner2012.title: Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database
spanner2012.author: James C. Corbett, Jeffrey Dean, Michael Epstein, Andrew Fikes, Christopher Frost, JJ Furman, Sanjay Ghemawat, Andrey Gubarev, Christopher Heiser, Peter Hochschild, Wilson Hsieh, Sebastian Kanthak, Eugene Kogan, Hongyi Li, Alexander Lloyd, Sergey Melnik, David Mwaura, David Nagle, Sean Quinlan, Rajesh Rao, Lindsay Rolig, Yasushi Saito, Michal Szymaniak, Christopher Taylor, Ruth Wang, Dale Woodford
spanner2012.venue: Proceedings of OSDI 2012 (10th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation), Hollywood, CA; section 5.4 'F1', page 11 of the PDF
spanner2012.quote: Spanner started being experimentally evaluated under production workloads in early 2011, as part of a rewrite of Google's advertising backend called F1 [35]. This backend was originally based on a MySQL database that was manually sharded many ways. The uncompressed dataset is tens of terabytes, which is small compared to many NoSQL instances, but was large enough to cause difficulties with sharded MySQL.
spanner2012.quote2: The MySQL sharding scheme assigned each customer and all related data to a fixed shard. This layout enabled the use of indexes and complex query processing on a per-customer basis, but required some knowledge of the sharding in application business logic.
spanner2012.quote3: Resharding this revenue-critical database as it grew in the number of customers and their data was extremely costly. The last resharding took over two years of intense effort, and involved coordination and testing across dozens of teams to minimize risk. This operation was too complex to do regularly: as a result, the team had to limit growth on the MySQL database by storing some data in external Bigtables, which compromised transactional behavior and the ability to query across all data.
spanner2012.quote4: The F1 team chose to use Spanner for several reasons. First, Spanner removes the need to manually reshard.
spanner2012.quote5: F1 has 2 replicas on the west coast of the US, and 3 on the east coast. ... Table 5 illustrates the distribution of the number of fragments per directory in F1. Each directory typically corresponds to a customer in the application stack above F1. The vast majority of directories (and therefore customers) consist of only 1 fragment, which means that reads and writes to those customers' data are guaranteed to occur on only a single server.
spanner2012.quote6: The F1 team, and Jeff Shute in particular, worked closely with us in developing our data model and helped immensely in tracking down performance and correctness bugs.
supports: AdWords' backend was manually sharded MySQL
the sharding scheme assigned each customer and all related data to a fixed shard
per-customer indexes and queries worked; the app had to know the sharding
the last resharding took over two years and dozens of teams
resharding was too complex to repeat, so growth on MySQL was capped and data went to external Bigtables
external Bigtables compromised transactional behavior and cross-data queries
Spanner removed the need to manually reshard
each Spanner directory typically corresponds to one customer
five F1 replicas, 2 west coast and 3 east coast

f12013.title: F1: A Distributed SQL Database That Scales
f12013.author: Jeff Shute, Radek Vingralek, Bart Samwel, Ben Handy, Chad Whipkey, Eric Rollins, Mircea Oancea, Kyle Littlefield, David Menestrina, Stephan Ellner, John Cieslewicz, Ian Rae, Traian Stancescu, Himani Apte
f12013.venue: Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, Vol. 6, No. 11, 2013 (PVLDB 6(11): 1068-1079)
f12013.quote: It was designed to replace a sharded MySQL implementation that was not able to meet our growing scalability and reliability requirements.
f12013.quote2: Our sharded database based on MySQL was hard to scale up, and even more difficult to rebalance. Our users needed complex queries and joins, which meant they had to carefully shard their data, and resharding data without breaking applications was challenging.
f12013.quote3: In AdWords, most transactions are typically updating data for a single advertiser at a time, so we made the advertiser a root table (Customer) and clustered related tables under it. This clustering was critical to achieving acceptable latency.
f12013.quote4: A row of the root table in the hierarchy is called a root row. All child table rows corresponding to a root row are clustered together with that root row in a single Spanner directory
supports: F1 replaced a sharded MySQL implementation
the sharded MySQL was hard to scale and harder to rebalance
AdWords made the advertiser the root table (Customer) because most transactions touch one advertiser
root row plus descendants live in one Spanner directory

f1sigmod2012.title: F1 - The Fault-Tolerant Distributed RDBMS Supporting Google's Ad Business (SIGMOD 2012 slide deck)
f1sigmod2012.author: Jeff Shute, Mircea Oancea, Stephan Ellner, Ben Handy, Eric Rollins, Bart Samwel, Radek Vingralek, Chad Whipkey, Xin Chen, Beat Jegerlehner, Kyle Littlefield, Phoenix Tong
f1sigmod2012.venue: SIGMOD 2012; slide deck archived at research.google (pubs/archive/38125.pdf), 19 pages, dated on its title slide 'SIGMOD May 22, 2012'
f1sigmod2012.quote: Our Legacy DB: Sharded MySQL | Sharding Strategy: Sharded by customer; Apps optimized using shard awareness | Limitations: Availability - Master / slave replication -> downtime during failover; Schema changes -> downtime for table locking. Scaling - Grow by adding shards; Rebalancing shards is extremely difficult and risky; Therefore, limit size and growth of data stored in database. Functionality - Can't do cross-shard transactions or joins
f1sigmod2012.quote2: Scale: 10s of TB, replicated to 1000s of machines
supports: the legacy AdWords DB was sharded by customer and apps were shard-aware
master/slave replication was filed under availability and caused downtime during failover
growth meant adding shards; rebalancing was extremely difficult and risky
the team therefore limited size and growth of stored data
f1sigmod2012.note: A slide deck, not a peer-reviewed paper: used only for the limitations list, which the peer-reviewed Spanner and F1 papers corroborate in prose. The prose's load-bearing claims all rest on spanner2012.

unverified: The calendar dates of the last resharding. The Spanner paper gives only its duration ('over two years') and that it was the most recent one before the F1 rewrite; no start or end date is published, so the prose gives a duration and never a date range.
How many engineers 'dozens of teams' amounts to. The paper counts teams, not people, and the prose does the same.

Which AdWords features were delayed or cancelled during the resharding. The paper names the consequence as capped growth on MySQL and data displaced into external Bigtables; it does not list shipped or unshipped features, and the prose claims no feature list.

That AdWords could not have bought a larger single MySQL machine. The sources say the dataset was 'tens of terabytes' and that the growth path was 'Grow by adding shards'; neither rules out vertical scaling explicitly, so the prose says only what the sources say.
Whether the 'external Bigtables' overflow was ever reabsorbed after the move to F1. Not stated in either paper.

Who physically delivered the SIGMOD 2012 talk. The archived deck is dated 'SIGMOD May 22, 2012' on its title slide and lists twelve authors led by Jeff Shute, but records no speaker; the cards therefore say first author, not presenter.
